note: The CQ MixPad Tutorial's lessons (Marko, 24.10.2026: 'Teach me by voice and mouse ... using this song as an example'). Coordinates are in a 1600 x 900 picture of the CQ MixPad window (title bar included), mapped onto the real window at play time. Steps: say (text, played from its pre-made mp3 in audio/), point (the mouse glides there, no click), click, live (orders to Ableton Live through the OSC router on 127.0.0.1:11002), wait (seconds). The tutorial only looks and listens: every click is a page, a bank or a listen key that is switched back. Nothing in the mix is changed.

lessons.title: 1. USB: how the computer and the CQ talk

steps.say: Lesson one. USB. Your CQ twelve T and the Mac are joined by one USB cable. That cable carries sixteen channels of sound in each direction at the same time. Sixteen go from the mixer to the computer, for recording. Sixteen come back from the computer to the mixer, for playback. In Ableton Live, the sixteen that go back to the mixer are called Ext. Out, one to sixteen.

This is the CONFIG page, INPUTS. These ten round sockets are your ten mono inputs. The small SD card and USB picture inside each one means the input is not listening to the socket on the back of the mixer. It is listening to the computer.

Down here is Input Source. Analogue means the XLR or jack socket on the back. SD and USB means the computer's channel with the same number. So Ableton's Ext. Out one plays on input one, Ext. Out two on input two, and so on up to ten. That is how Svemir's voice, the bass and the percussion of the Santoshi concert reach your faders.
Channels eleven to sixteen are three stereo pairs, and this tab decides what they carry. Eleven and twelve are set to ST IN.
Thirteen and fourteen.

And fifteen and sixteen, the main mix. Going to the computer, each pair records what is chosen here. Coming back from the computer, I measured it on the meters: eleven and twelve play on the ST IN channel, thirteen and fourteen play on the channel called USB, and fifteen and sixteen are the main mix.

This is the PROCESSING page, bank ST IN and FX. Here are three stereo channels side by side: ST IN, USB and BT, Bluetooth. Now I send the venue's own mix from Live to Ext. Out thirteen. Watch the small meter of the USB channel.
There it moves. The fader of the USB channel stays down at off. That keeps the venue sound out of your main mix and out of the SD recording.
To hear it anyway, press the headphone key on top of the channel. It is called listen. It puts that channel alone in your headphones, even with its fader down. I press it now.
Now your headphones play the venue mix. Compare it with your own mix. I press listen again, and the headphones go back to your main mix.

That was lesson one. One cable, sixteen channels each way. Inputs one to ten come from Ext. Out one to ten when their source is SD and USB. Thirteen and fourteen land on the USB channel. Listen puts any channel in your headphones without touching the mix.
Lesson two. The map of the mixer. Everything in CQ MixPad sits in the same places on every page. Across the top are five pages.
CONFIG is the wiring. Which socket or USB channel feeds each input, the outputs, USB and Bluetooth, and the network. You set it once for a show.
PROCESSING is the sound of each channel. Gain, the high pass filter, the gate, the equaliser, the compressor and the sends. This is where a voice becomes clear.
FADER is the mixing desk itself. A fader, pan and mute for each channel. During the concert you live here.
FX holds the two effect units. Unit one is easy verb, a reverb. Unit two is echo verb.
The big knob is the size of the room. The type sits to its right; ours is Vocal Classic.
HOME is the house. Recording to the SD card, the scenes where a whole mix is stored, data, and the system.
And here, the headphone volume.
Down the left side are the banks. Inputs one to five.
Inputs six to ten.
The stereo channels and the effect returns.
The outputs, six monitor outputs and the main.
And the mute groups and DCAs, which move several channels with one fader.
Custom is your own layer, where you can put any eight channels you like side by side.
The three keys at the top left are soft keys. You decide what they do, for example start the recording.
On the right is always the fader of the channel you selected last, big, so you can set it finely.
And above it, Sends To. Normally it says Main LR, and the faders mix the main. Switch it to a monitor output or to an effect, and the same faders now set what goes there. That was lesson two.

Lesson three. Routing. Every sound in the mixer travels the same road. It comes in through an input, it is shaped in processing, and then it is sent out. Into the main mix, into monitor outputs, into the effects, into the headphones, and to the computer.
The road starts here, with the input source. Analogue for a microphone on stage, SD and USB for a recording played from the computer, as we do with Santoshi.
This is where it ends. Main LR feeds the big speakers and the SD recording. Out one to six are for stage monitors, or for a second recorder.

To build a monitor mix, choose the output in Sends To, and the input faders become the levels for that monitor. Choose Main LR again to come back. The effects work the same way: Sends To FX one, and the faders become how much of each voice goes into the reverb. That is how the three voices got their reverb, at about minus thirteen.
On the CONFIG page, OUTPUTS, the headphone output is set to Listen. When no listen key is pressed you hear the main mix. Press a listen key and you hear that channel alone.

And to the computer, the USB tab. Multitrack sends every input on its own channel, so Ableton can record them all. The source point decides whether the computer gets the input clean, or with your processing on it.
Last, the SD card. HOME, RECORD. Here the main mix is recorded in stereo while you mix, the way you want to record the Santoshi mix. That was lesson three.
Lesson four. Making the Santoshi mix good. I start the concert in Live from the first song, Jai Ganesha.

First the order. In devotional music the voices carry everything, so we mix voices first, then the rhythm, then the colour. In Live every clip already plays at the same level, minus twelve, and every fader in Live is at zero. So all the mixing happens here, on the CQ.
Every channel reads from top to bottom. The name. The listen key. The picture, which opens the processing: gain, high pass filter, gate, equaliser and compressor. The sends. And the fader.

I now solo Svemir's voice in Live, so only that channel plays into the mixer. Listen to it alone. Is it clear? Is there rumble under it? The high pass filter removes the rumble below the voice. The vocal preset already has a gentle compressor, so the soft words and the strong words come closer together.

Solo off. Now the method. Bring Svemir's voice to about zero on the fader. Then bring Igor's voice and Tajana's voice up until they sit with it, not under it and not over it. When all voices are understood, bring in the percussion. Mridangam, mridangam low and djembe, until the rhythm carries the voices without covering them.
Then the bass and the guitar, the snoopy DI and Igor's DI. Bass is felt more than heard. If the voices become muddy, the bass is too loud.
Watch the main meter on the right. The loudest moments should touch about zero, never the red. If everything is too loud, bring all faders down together, never the main above zero.

Now the test. Press listen on the USB channel, and you hear what the venue's own mixer made of the same concert. Release it and you hear yours. Go back and forth during a whole song. Where is your voice louder, where is theirs clearer? That is the best teacher you have tonight.

When the mix is good, store it. HOME, SCENES, select Santoshi Mix, and press Overwrite. Then the whole mix comes back in one touch at the next rehearsal. Then record the main to the SD card under HOME, RECORD, from the first song to the last. That was lesson four, and the end of the tutorial.
